routes.label: Use a unit-circle polynomial and its conjugate

question: For real numbers \(x,\) let \[ \begin{aligned} P(x) &= 1 + \cos(x) + i\sin(x) \\ &\quad {}- \cos(2x) - i\sin(2x) \\ &\quad {}+ \cos(3x) + i\sin(3x) \end{aligned} \] where \(i = \sqrt{-1}.\) For how many values of \(x\) with \(0 \le x \lt 2\pi\) does \[P(x) = 0?\]
solution:
The imaginary part is easier to factor than the full expression, and every zero of \(P(x)\) must make it vanish.

Write
\[
R(x)=1+\cos x-\cos 2x+\cos 3x,
\qquad
I(x)=\sin x-\sin 2x+\sin 3x.
\]
A complex number is zero exactly when both its real and imaginary parts are zero. The angle-addition formulas give
\[
\sin x+\sin 3x
=\sin(2x-x)+\sin(2x+x)
=2\sin 2x\cos x.
\]
Consequently,
\[
I(x)=\sin 2x(2\cos x-1).
\]
Thus either \(\sin 2x=0\), giving
\[
x=0,\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \frac{3\pi}{2},
\]
or \(\cos x=\frac12\), giving
\[
x=\frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{5\pi}{3}.
\]
These are all the possibilities in \(0\le x<2\pi\). Substitution into the real part gives:

| Possible \(x\) | \(R(x)\) |
|---|---:|
| \(0,\ \pi/2,\ 3\pi/2\) | \(2\) |
| \(\pi\) | \(-2\) |
| \(\pi/3,\ 5\pi/3\) | \(1\) |

For the last row, the three cosines are \(\frac12,-\frac12,-1\), so \(R(x)=1+\frac12+\frac12-1=1\).

The real part never vanishes at a candidate. Therefore there are \(\boxed{0}\) values of \(x\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The trigonometric terms are powers of one unit complex number, so conjugation can turn the equation into a second polynomial equation.

Let
\[
z=\cos x+i\sin x.
\]
Then \(|z|=1\), and the angle-addition formulas give \(z^k=\cos(kx)+i\sin(kx)\) for \(k=2,3\). Hence \(P(x)=0\) would imply
\[
f(z)=1+z-z^2+z^3=0.
\]
The conjugate \(\overline z=\cos x-i\sin x\) satisfies \(z\overline z=1\), so \(\overline z=1/z\). Conjugating the equation, which replaces each occurrence of \(i\) by \(-i\) and preserves sums and products, gives
\[
1+\frac1z-\frac1{z^2}+\frac1{z^3}=0.
\]
Multiplication by \(z^3\) yields
\[
z^3+z^2-z+1=0.
\]
Subtracting the original equation now gives
\[
2z^2-2z=2z(z-1)=0.
\]
Since \(|z|=1\), we have \(z\ne0\), so \(z=1\). But \(f(1)=2\), a contradiction.

Thus \(P(x)\) has no zeros in the required interval. The answer is \(\boxed{0}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Compare conjugate equations
